newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss hurry to catch up in Euro telecoms sale.
newsitem.headline: Swiss hurry to catch up in Euro telecoms sale.

text.p: Officials at Swiss state telecommunications provider Telecom PTT said the company would pick up the pace of its restructuring ahead of plans for a partial privatisation in the second half of 1998.

"No other company has had to do so much in such a small amount of time -- dividing up the whole enterprise, setting up a new organisation, readying for a bourse flotation, while at the same time establishing and implementing a new strategy," Swiss Telecom chief executive Felix Rosenberg told reporters.
"We have already lost some time," he added.
Even if all goes as planned, the Swiss telecom provider is already well behind Britain and Germany, where privatisation is completed, as well as France, where it is under way.
Spain is considering bringing forward privatisation to January 1998 from December 1998.

Telecom's IPO will also be at least half a year after deregulation of the European Union telecom market set for 1998, which is expected to bring increased competition for European telecom providers. Switzerland, which is not part of the EU, is timing reforms to coincide with the EU liberalisation.

Telecom plans to bring forward to April an internal restructuring originally planned for October, and will also change its name to Swisscom in October 1997. It is going ahead with plans to restructure its tariffs in August.

The tariff changes are expected to lead to 200 million Swiss francs ($137 million) in lost revenues in 1997, which will mean revenues of 10.2 billion for this year. Telecom expects profits of around 1.5 billion in 1997 versus 700 million in 1996. The 1997 figure excludes any eventual costs tied to restructuring.

Telecom is also looking to expand further service outside Switzerland to offset the expected loss of 15 to 20 percent of its domestic market share over the next five years due to increasing internationalisation of the telecoms market, according to Serge Chammartin, head of finance for Telecom.

Parliament is set to give final approval next month to splitting the telecom and communications activities from the rest of the state postal operations, which include everything from mail delivery to giro accounts and the postal bus service.
According to the Swiss constitution, up to 49 percent of the resulting telecommunications concern can be privatised.
Telecom officials declined to elaborate on plans for the initial public offering, focusing instead on the changes needed to make Telecom a viable competitor.

"An IPO will be possible in the second half of 1998 at the earliest. The timing is still open. It depends in particular on the federal government's objectives, Telecom PTT's capital requirements and the state of capital markets," said Chammartin.
Telecom said that one source of concern was its relatively low ratio of equity to debt, currently 10 percent.

Alongside plans to increase sales and profits, a third objective "is repaying debt and thus improving our financial situation. In the run-up to partial privatisation, the equity ratio is to be increased considerably," Chammartin said.
The goal here would be to increase the level to something closer to 20 to 30 percent, in line with competitors.
At the same time, Telecom did not rule out further job reductions, partly as a result of attrition.
"We are already efficient but that doesn't mean we have done everything with respect to jobs," Rosenberg said. It employs roughly 60,000 people now.
